summary: Arabic marks a definite noun with the prefix al- (الْ), written joined to the noun, and an indefinite noun with nunation (tanwīn: -un, -an, -in). There is no word for “a”. Before the 14 sun letters (ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن) the l of al- is assimilated: it carries no sukūn and the next letter gets a šadda — الثُّومُ = aṯ-ṯūmu. Diptotes (طَمَاطِم، بَطَاطِس، سَبَانِخ) never take tanwīn, and indeclinable words in -ā / -ī (كُوسَا، بْرُوكُلِي) show definiteness only by al-. General statements (“I like tomatoes”) use al-: أُحِبُّ الطَّمَاطِمَ.

askYourself: Is the noun specific (one we both know) or meant in general (“tomatoes”, “onions as food”)? → al-
Is it one of many, not identified (“a carrot”)? → tanwīn, no al-
Does the noun start with a sun letter? → no sukūn on the l, šadda on the letter (الطَّمَاطِمُ)
Is the noun a diptote or indeclinable? → no tanwīn even when it is indefinite
After adding al-, did I remove the tanwīn?
steps: Choose the case ending (-u nominative, -a accusative, -i genitive).
Write al- (sun or moon letter rule) or the tanwīn form.

traps: Generic = definite: هِيَ تُحِبُّ الْخِيَارَ = she likes cucumbers (in general), not only “the cucumbers”.
هٰذِهِ جَزَرَةٌ (“this is a carrot” — a sentence) vs هٰذِهِ الْجَزَرَةُ (“this carrot” — a phrase): the article changes the structure.
What you have with عِنْدَ is indefinite and nominative: عِنْدِي جَزَرَةٌ.
With a sun letter you hear no l: الطَّمَاطِمُ = aṭ-ṭamāṭimu.
